ABSTRACT In the situation of mass vaccination against COVID-19, few studies have reported on the early kinetics of specific antibodies (IgG/IgM/IgA) of vaccine breakthrough cases. There is still a lack of epidemiological evidence about the value of serological indicators in the auxiliary diagnosis of COVID-19 infection, especially when the nucleic acid results were undetectable. Omicron breakthrough cases post-inactivated vaccination ( n = 456) and COVID-19-naive individuals with two doses of inactivated vaccination ( n = 693) were enrolled. Blood samples were collected and tested for SARS-CoV-2 antibody levels based on the magnetic chemiluminescence enzyme immunoassay. Among Omicron breakthrough cases, the serum IgG antibody level was 36.34 Sample/CutOff (S/CO) (95% confidence interval [CI], 31.89 to 40.79) in the acute phase and 88.45 S/CO (95% CI, 82.79 to 94.12) in the recovery phase. Serum IgA can be detected in the first week post-symptom onset (PSO) and showed an almost linear increase within 5 weeks PSO. Compared with those of breakthrough cases, IgG and IgA titers of the postimmune group were much lower (4.70 S/CO and 0.46 S/CO, respectively). Multivariate regression showed that serum IgG and IgA levels in Omicron breakthrough cases were mainly affected by the weeks PSO ( P < 0.001). Receiver operating characteristic ROC0 curve analysis showed that the area under the curve (AUC) was 0.744 and 0.806 when the cutoff values of IgA and IgG were 1 S/CO and 15 S/CO, respectively. Omicron breakthrough infection can lead to a further increase in IgG and IgA levels relative to those of the immunized population. When nucleic acid real-time PCR was negative, we would use the kinetics of IgG and IgA levels to distinguish the breakthrough cases from the immunized population. IMPORTANCE This study fills a gap in the epidemiological evidence by investigating the value of serological indicators, particularly IgG and IgA levels, in the auxiliary diagnosis of COVID-19 infections when nucleic acid results are undetectable. The findings reveal that among Omicron breakthrough cases, both IgG and IgA antibody levels exhibit significant changes. Serum IgG levels increase during the acute phase and rise further in the recovery phase. Serum IgA can be detected as early as the first week post-symptom onset (PSO), showing a consistent linear increase within 5 weeks PSO. Furthermore, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis demonstrates the potential of IgG and IgA cutoff values as diagnostic markers. The study’s conclusion underscores the importance of monitoring IgG and IgA kinetics in distinguishing Omicron breakthrough cases from vaccinated individuals. These findings contribute to the development of more accurate diagnostic approaches and help inform public health strategies during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. The Omicron variant has been detected in several countries and regions around the world ( 2 ). SARS-CoV-2 vaccines are effective in reducing the risk of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection and progression to severe COVID-19 ( 3 ). However, as antibody titers wane over time, the vaccine effectiveness decreases ( 4 , 5 ). This provides suboptimal protection against emerging variants with immune escape potential, such as Omicron, leading to breakthrough infections and reinfections ( 6 – 10 ). As vaccination for SARS-CoV-2 becomes increasingly available and the number of breakthrough cases continues to increase, it will be useful to understand the kinetics of antibodies in postvaccination and breakthrough infection populations. It is also worth exploring whether there are differences between the characteristics of humoral immunity in these two representative populations and in those of previously studied naturally infected individuals. For example, Cheng et al. monitored BBIBP vaccine-induced virus-specific antibody levels (SARS-CoV-2-IgA/IgM/IgG) over multiple time points and showed that serum antibody levels decreased over time ( 11 ). Further, Ma et al. reached a similar conclusion that the levels of receptor-binding domain (RBD) antibodies and IgG peaked 1 month after the second injection, while IgM and IgA levels remained consistently low throughout the course of vaccination ( 12 ). For naturally infected individuals (those without prevaccination), previous studies have shown that antibodies caused by SARS-CoV-2 appear 3 days after the onset of symptoms or 1 week after infection ( 13 , 14 ). Our team also suggested in a previous study that, at a median follow-up of up to 15.6 months in a naturally infected population, 80.19% of patients were IgG positive and 20.44% were IgM positive ( 15 ). Through an extensive literature search, Koutsakos et al. indicated that immune recall following breakthrough infection varies in timing and magnitude. In addition, Omicron breakthrough infection elicits less extensive immune recall than Delta ( 16 ). Yadav et al. assessed the sera of naive, recovered, and breakthrough patients vaccinated with Covaxin for their neutralizing ability against the Omicron variant ( 17 ). Important aspects of humoral immunity, such as the kinetics of IgG, IgM, and IgA over time after vaccination or post-symptom onset/infection (PSO), were neglected. There is still a lack of epidemiological evidence regarding the value of serological indicators in the auxiliary diagnosis of COVID-19, especially when nucleic acid results are undetectable. Therefore, a case-control study was conducted using Omicron breakthrough cases with inactivated vaccine and COVID-19-naive individuals with two doses of inactivated vaccine as the control group in Jiangsu Province, China. Our aim was first to capture the precise kinetics of specific antibodies in Omicron breakthrough cases in the acute and recovery phases and to compare them with those of the postimmune population. Second, we explored whether the quantitative levels of IgG/IgM/IgA played a role in distinguishing between these antibodies induced by vaccine-only or vaccine-infection dual function. Third, we attempted to determine the exposure time of infected individuals during a large epidemic of the Omicron variant.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the early kinetics and diagnostic value of SARS-CoV-2 specific antibodies (IgG, IgM, IgA) in Omicron breakthrough cases following inactivated vaccination, comparing them with COVID-19-naive individuals who received two doses of inactivated vaccine. The findings reveal significant differences in antibody levels and kinetics, with breakthrough cases exhibiting robust and increasing IgG and IgA responses in the acute and recovery phases. Both IgG and IgA demonstrate diagnostic potential for distinguishing breakthrough infections, especially when nucleic acid test results are undetectable, with highest antibody levels observed during the recovery phase and a rapid increase within the first two weeks post-symptom onset.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Immune response to SARS-CoV-2 Omicron breakthrough infection following inactivated vaccination.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: The study involved 456 Omicron breakthrough cases and 693 COVID-19-naive individuals, all of whom had received two doses of inactivated SARS-CoV-2 vaccine; less than 50% of breakthrough cases received a homologous booster. Serum antibody levels were measured using magnetic chemiluminescence enzyme immunoassay. The median interval from the last vaccine dose to symptom onset in breakthrough cases was 5.45 months (acute phase) and 4.22 months (recovery phase), while for the postimmune group, blood collection was 2.67 months post-last dose. No specific dose-response comparisons for vaccination were reported; instead, the study focused on comparing antibody kinetics and levels between different infection phases and vaccinated states.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Antibody Level and Positivity Rate)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in recovery and acute phases of Omicron breakthrough cases compared to the postimmune vaccinated population, with a rapid increase post-symptom onset and a sharp decrease post-vaccination in the postimmune group.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: In Omicron breakthrough cases, IgG was 36.34 S/CO (95% CI, 31.89 to 40.79) in the acute phase and 88.45 S/CO (95% CI, 82.79 to 94.12) in the recovery phase. In the postimmune group, IgG was 4.70 S/CO (95% CI, 4.18 to 5.21). Positivity rates were 83.77% (acute breakthrough), 97.97% (recovery breakthrough), and 76.19% (postimmune), with significant differences (P < 0.001). Levels sharply rose to 80.45 S/CO in the second week PSO and peaked at 103.84 S/CO in the fourth week PSO in breakthrough cases. In the postimmune group, levels dropped from 13.81 to 3.63 S/CO in the first 2 months post-vaccination, reaching 1.07 S/CO in the 8th month. 50% of breakthrough cases showed a 4-fold or higher increase in recovery/acute phase, with a negative correlation between acute IgG levels and the recovery/acute ratio (r=-0.8917, P < 0.0001). Estimated half-life is 100-230 days. A diagnostic cutoff of 15 S/CO had 67.98% sensitivity, 93.22% specificity, and an AUC of 0.806.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mediates long-term humoral immunity, adaptive immune response, and immune memory, providing sustained protection and immune control against SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Omicron BA.2 breakthrough infection (acute and recovery phases) following inactivated vaccination, compared to COVID-19-naive individuals with two doses of inactivated vaccination. Levels are influenced by weeks post-symptom onset, age, booster dose status, and acute/convalescent patient status.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as an auxiliary diagnostic marker for COVID-19 infection, especially when nucleic acid results are undetectable. Higher levels and a rapid increase indicate an Omicron breakthrough infection compared to vaccination alone, reflecting enhanced immune recall and offering protective benefits during reinfection.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Antibody Level and Positivity Rate)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in the recovery phase of Omicron breakthrough cases, but no significant difference between the acute phase of breakthrough cases and the postimmune vaccinated population. Levels were low and often undetectable in breakthrough cases over time, and fluctuated at low levels in the postimmune population.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Positivity rates were 13.31% (acute breakthrough), 33.78% (recovery breakthrough), and 8.23% (postimmune), with significant differences (P < 0.001). Antibody levels (S/CO) were 0.61 (acute breakthrough), 1.27 (recovery breakthrough), and 0.50 (postimmune), with no significant difference between acute breakthrough and postimmune (P > 0.05). Levels were low and undetectable within 5 weeks post-symptom onset in breakthrough cases, and fluctuated at low levels (<1 S/CO) in the postimmune group. IgM typically rises to near peak state in the second week after onset in general infection, but does not rapidly increase after antigen reexposure in vaccinated individuals. Estimated half-life is 55 days.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Mediates the primary and early adaptive humoral immune response to initial exposure to pathogens, contributing to early immune control of infection.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Omicron BA.2 breakthrough infection (acute and recovery phases) following inactivated vaccination, compared to COVID-19-naive individuals with two doses of inactivated vaccination. Measured during acute phase of infection.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an early or acute phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination response. It is less indicative of secondary immunization/immune recall compared to IgG in vaccinated individuals.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Serum (also distributed in blood and mucous membranes)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Protein Level (Antibody Level and Positivity Rate)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Higher in recovery phase of Omicron breakthrough cases compared to acute phase and the postimmune vaccinated population. Levels were detectable from the first week post-symptom onset and showed an almost linear increase within 5 weeks PSO in breakthrough cases, while fluctuating at low levels in the postimmune population.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Positivity rates were 39.61% (acute breakthrough), 88.51% (recovery breakthrough), and 6.64% (postimmune), with significant differences (P < 0.001). Antibody levels (S/CO) were 3.13 (acute breakthrough), 10.11 (recovery breakthrough), and 0.46 (postimmune) (P < 0.001). In breakthrough cases, IgA was detected from the first week PSO and increased linearly within 5 weeks PSO. The positivity rate in the first week for breakthrough cases was 34.10%. Levels in the postimmune group fluctuated at low levels (<1 S/CO). The factor affecting IgA levels was mainly weeks after symptom onset (P < 0.001). Estimated half-life is 42 days (spike-binding) or 210 days (general IgA over 8 months). A diagnostic cutoff of 1 S/CO had 55.48% sensitivity, 93.36% specificity, and an AUC of 0.744.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Provides local mucosal immunity, particularly at epithelial surfaces like the respiratory tract, and plays a role in the systemic adaptive immune response, contributing to immune control and protection against reinfection.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Omicron BA.2 breakthrough infection (acute and recovery phases) following inactivated vaccination, compared to COVID-19-naive individuals with two doses of inactivated vaccination. Levels are influenced by weeks post-symptom onset.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as an auxiliary diagnostic marker for COVID-19 infection, especially when nucleic acid results are undetectable. Detectable and increasing levels post-symptom onset indicate an Omicron breakthrough infection compared to vaccination alone, important for mucosal and systemic immune response.
